rows.label: Typical-year hourly weather and solar, central London (51.507, −0.128)

source.title: PVGIS v5.3 typical meteorological year (European Commission Joint Research Centre)

rows.rationale: Fetched at build time by scripts/fetch-pvgis.ts and trimmed to four columns: T2m (air temperature, °C), G(h) (global horizontal), Gb(n) (beam normal) and Gd(h) (diffuse horizontal) irradiance in W/m². Timestamps are UTC, as PVGIS gives them; there are 8,760 hours with no leap day. Each month comes from a different source year, listed in the snapshot's monthsSelected.

rows.label: Offset added to every hourly outdoor temperature
rows.rationale: Zero for the typical year. Tests set it below zero to build a colder year and check that heat demand rises.

rows.label: Minutes past the hour at which the snapshot's irradiance values apply
rows.rationale: The engine places the sun at this time within each UTC hour when it splits irradiance onto walls. The PVGIS typical year labels each hour HH:00. The 10 minutes is inferred from the data, not from PVGIS documentation: checked on the snapshot on 18 October 2026: global horizontal should equal beam normal × cos(zenith) + diffuse horizontal, and the mean absolute mismatch, as a share of annual global irradiance, is 1.5% with the sun at HH:00, 0.24% at HH:10 and 2.6% at HH:30. A test repeats this check.

rows.label: House type of each archetype
rows.rationale: The archetype set agreed in the phase 2 spec (SPECIFICATIONS/02-complete-v1-model.md, "House types and geometry"). A bungalow is taken as detached, with no party wall.

rows.label: RdSAP age band of each archetype
rows.rationale: Each archetype is keyed to one England age band in RdSAP 10 Table 1: A before 1900, C 1930–49, D 1950–66, E 1967–75, F 1976–82, G 1983–90, K 2007–11, L 2012–22. The spec names L as 2012–21; RdSAP 10 runs it to 2022.

rows.label: Storeys of each archetype
rows.rationale: Two storeys for every house, one for the bungalow. Rooms in the roof and basements are left out.

rows.label: Wall construction of each archetype
rows.rationale: Solid brick for the houses built before 1900, cavity masonry for the rest, as named in the spec. The wall construction decides which wall answers are offered and the party wall U-value.

rows.label: Default total floor area of each archetype

source.title: MHCLG: Floor Space in English Homes, main report figures and tables (English Housing Survey 2012), Figures 3.3–3.7

rows.rationale: English Housing Survey 2012 mean usable floor area for the type and age, rounded to 1 m²: mid-terrace pre-1919 87.4; end-terrace pre-1919 103.6; semi 1945–64 88.3; bungalow 1945–64 73.3; mid-terrace 1965–74 80.3; detached 1975–80 130.9; detached 1981–90 133.9; semi post-2002 84.9; mid-terrace post-2002 86.3. The 1930s semi keeps phase 1's 90 m² (the EHS mean for 1919–44 semis is 93.8), so its NEED readings and calibration target stay those of phase 1. Floor area is a fixed input for a run, not sampled.
rows.overrideHint: Use the total floor area on your EPC.

rows.label: Default number of bedrooms of each archetype
rows.rationale: The bedroom count with the most homes in NEED's 2024 London rows for the archetype's property type and NEED age band (gas present, standard meter). It picks reading T in scripts/archetypes/needReadings.ts.

rows.label: Footprint depth ÷ width of each archetype
rows.rationale: Width is the frontage; depth runs front to back, along any party wall. Terraces are narrow and deep (2.0 for pre-1900, 1.5–1.6 later); semis are close to square (1.1–1.2), giving the 1930s semi a 6.4 m × 7.0 m footprint and about 20 m of exposed perimeter, as in phase 1; detached houses and the bungalow are wider than deep (0.8).

rows.label: Number of party walls of each archetype
rows.rationale: Two for a mid-terrace, one for an end-terrace or semi, none for a detached house or bungalow. Each party wall runs the depth of the house.

rows.label: Default loft insulation answer of each archetype
rows.rationale: About 100 mm for the archetypes built before 1991: RdSAP 10 Table 18 assumes 100 mm for age bands A–G when the thickness is unknown, noting that most lofts have at least that. 270 mm or more for the 2007–11 and 2012 onwards archetypes, the Table 18 value for bands K and L as built.

rows.label: Default wall insulation answer of each archetype
rows.rationale: "Cavity filled" for the cavity archetypes built before 1991 (bands C–G). In 2024, 73% of owner-occupied dwellings with cavity walls had cavity wall insulation (60% of private rented and 79% of social housing), so filled is the most common answer. The survey gives no split by age band; the same share is assumed for every band C–G. "As built" for the solid brick archetypes, whose walls are mostly uninsulated, and for bands K and L, which were insulated as built (the survey, like SAP, assumes cavity walls built after 1995 are insulated). Decided by Magnus on 18 October 2026 after the first archetype table had run with unfilled cavities, so the choice was made with both results in view (see scripts/archetypes/README.md). Source checked on 19 October 2026.

source.title: MHCLG: English Housing Survey 2024 to 2025, headline findings on housing quality and energy efficiency, Chapter 2 (Figure 2.8, Annex Table 2.10)

rows.label: Default glazing answer of each archetype
rows.rationale: Older double glazing (installed before 2002) for the archetypes built before 1991, as most original single glazing has been replaced; newer double glazing for the 2007–11 and 2012 onwards archetypes, which were built with it.

rows.label: Default room height by age band
rows.rationale: RdSAP measures room heights on site and has no default table. RdSAP 10 calls 2.4 m a normal room height (section 3.9), used here from 1950. Victorian houses have higher ceilings (2.7 m); the 1930s semi keeps phase 1's 2.5 m.

rows.label: Height added to each room height above the lowest storey
rows.rationale: RdSAP 10 section 3.6: 0.25 m is added to each room height except the lowest storey to give the storey height, for the floor void. Storey heights set the gross wall area and the heated volume.

rows.label: Window area per m² of floor area, by age band (houses)

source.title: RdSAP 2012 version 9.93 specification (BRE, 19 November 2017), Table S4

rows.rationale: RdSAP 2012 Table S4, house or bungalow: window area = slope × total floor area + intercept. RdSAP 10 measures every window instead and has no default formula, so the RdSAP 2012 formula, from the same stock survey basis, stands in. Checked line by line on 18 October 2026.

rows.label: Window area intercept, by age band (houses)

source.title: RdSAP 2012 version 9.93 specification (BRE, 19 November 2017), Table S4

rows.rationale: RdSAP 2012 Table S4, house or bungalow (see archetypes.windowAreaSlope). Checked line by line on 18 October 2026.

rows.label: Default wall thickness, by construction and age band
rows.rationale: RdSAP 10 Table 3, England. It sets the solid brick wall U-value (Table 13) and enters the ground floor calculation.

rows.label: Ground floor construction when unknown, by age band
rows.rationale: RdSAP 10 Table 19: suspended timber for bands A and B, solid from band C. Many 1930s houses have suspended timber floors in practice; RdSAP's default is used.

rows.label: All-over ground floor insulation when unknown, by age band
rows.rationale: RdSAP 10 Table 19, England and Wales.

rows.label: SAP occupancy formula coefficients
rows.rationale: SAP 10.2 Table 1b: N = base + saturation × [1 − exp(−curvature × (TFA − minimumFloorArea)²)] + slope × (TFA − minimumFloorArea), and N = 1 at or below the minimum. An archetype's default occupant count is N for its floor area, rounded, within 1–5.

rows.label: External door area
rows.rationale: RdSAP 10 section 3.7: an external door can be taken as 1.85 m². One external door, as in phase 1.

rows.label: Fabric quality factor (one multiplier on every U-value and the air change rate)

source.title: In-situ measurements of wall U-values in English housing (BRE for DECC, 2015)

rows.rationale: One shared factor, so independent draws of each U-value cannot average out and narrow the band. BRE found RdSAP's old solid-wall default was pessimistic by about a quarter, so the range reaches down to 0.75 (stock better than the tables) and up to 1.15 (worse, for example from poor workmanship). The mode is 1.0, the tables as given.

rows.label: External wall U-value, by age band, construction and wall answer
rows.rationale: RdSAP 10 Table 6 (England), checked line by line on 18 October 2026. Solid brick as built in band A: Table 13 for a 220 mm wall (Table 3), 1.7. Solid wall insulated: section 5.8 with the 50 mm row that Table 6 says to use when the thickness is unknown, 1 ÷ (1/1.7 + 1.5) = 0.48. Cavity as built and filled from Table 6. A filled cavity is not offered for bands K and L, which Table 6 treats as insulated as built. Fabric uncertainty is carried by fabric.qualityFactor.
rows.overrideHint: Use the U-value from a survey if you have one.

rows.label: Party wall U-value, by wall construction
rows.rationale: RdSAP 10 Table 15: 0 for solid masonry; 0.25 for a house whose party wall construction cannot be determined, used for the cavity archetypes (an unfilled cavity party wall is 0.5, a filled one 0.2). A cavity party wall loses heat through air movement in the cavity, which is why it is not zero.

rows.label: Window U-value (PVC or wooden frame), by glazing answer
rows.rationale: RdSAP 10 Table 24, whole-window U-values before the curtain adjustment: single glazing 4.8; double glazing installed before 2002 with a 12 mm gap 2.8 (the row RdSAP uses when the installation date is unknown); double or triple glazing installed 2002 or later 2.0. The engine applies fabric.windowCurtainResistance on top.
rows.overrideHint: Use the U-value from your window certificate if you have one.

rows.label: Thermal resistance added to windows for curtains and blinds
rows.rationale: SAP 10.2 section 3.2, formula (2): the effective window U-value is 1 ÷ (1/U + 0.04), a curtain resistance of 0.08 halved because curtains are open half the time. RdSAP 10 Table 24 applies it to its window values.

rows.label: External door U-value, by age band
rows.rationale: RdSAP 10 Table 26, a door to the outside: 3.0 for bands A–J, 2.0 for K, 1.8 for L (England).

rows.label: Roof U-value at the ceiling, by loft insulation answer
rows.rationale: RdSAP 10 Table 16, insulation at joists at ceiling level: none 2.3, 100 mm 0.40, 270 mm 0.16. Checked line by line on 18 October 2026.
rows.overrideHint: Measure the loft insulation depth if you can.

rows.label: Thermal bridging factor y, by age band
rows.rationale: RdSAP 10 Table 21: 0.15 for bands A–I, 0.11 for J, 0.08 for K–M. Heat loss through junctions between elements, added as y × the total exposed area of walls, windows, door, roof and ground floor (SAP 10.2 Appendix K).

rows.label: Air change rate (infiltration and ventilation), by age band
rows.rationale: Phase 1's 1.0 for a 1930s house with a suspended or solid floor, a chimney and some draughtproofing (HEM worked out about 0.89 for it). Higher for a Victorian house with sash windows and open flues, falling as construction tightens: about 0.8 for the 1970s–80s, and 0.5–0.6 for houses built to the 2006 and 2010 airtightness rules with intermittent extract fans. RdSAP 10 Table 5 instead builds the rate from the SAP 10.2 ventilation worksheet, which needs data about chimneys, fans and draughtproofing that the quick facts do not ask.

rows.label: Thermal mass parameter (heat capacity per m² of floor), by wall construction
rows.rationale: RdSAP 10 section 5.16, Table 22: 250 kJ/m²K for masonry (stone, solid brick, cavity walls, system built) without internal insulation; 100 kJ/m²K for timber frame, or masonry with internal insulation. Every archetype is masonry. The 'solid wall insulated' answer is taken as external insulation, which keeps the 250. The engine's heat capacity C is this × the floor area (SAP 10.2 defines the parameter as heat capacity ÷ total floor area, counting internal walls and floors). Checked against the PDF on 20 October 2026.

rows.label: Ground floor U-value parameters (BS EN ISO 13370 as RdSAP applies it)
rows.rationale: RdSAP 10 section 5.12: clay soil (1.5 W/m·K); Rsi 0.17 and Rse 0.04 m²K/W; floor insulation 0.035 W/m·K; for a suspended floor, deck resistance 0.2 m²K/W, height above ground 0.3 m, wind speed 5 m/s, wind shielding factor 0.05, ventilation openings 0.003 m² per m of exposed perimeter, and underfloor wall U-value 1.5 W/m²K. Units: conductivities in W/m·K, resistances in m²K/W, height in m, wind speed in m/s, openings in m²/m. The engine computes the floor U-value from these, the floor area, the exposed perimeter and the wall thickness, and rounds it to 2 decimal places as RdSAP does.

rows.label: Window frame factor (glazed share of the window area)
rows.rationale: RdSAP 10 Table 24 note: frame factor 0.7 for a wooden or PVC frame (0.8 for metal). Checked on 18 October 2026.

rows.label: Solar access (overshading) factor for windows
rows.rationale: SAP 10.2 Table 6d, winter solar access factor for average or unknown overshading (20–60% of sky blocked), which RdSAP 10 section 7 uses for every dwelling. Checked on 18 October 2026.

rows.label: Ground reflectance (albedo) seen by the walls
rows.rationale: The conventional value for snow-free ground in the isotropic-sky model, which the engine uses to put irradiance on the walls. A wall sees half the ground, so it receives 0.1 × global horizontal irradiance by reflection. Grass and paving range from about 0.1 to 0.3.

rows.label: Window solar transmittance at normal incidence (g⊥), by glazing answer
rows.rationale: RdSAP 10 Table 24: single 0.85, double before 2002 0.76, double or triple 2002 or later 0.72. SAP's 0.9 factor for non-normal incidence (gains.nonNormalIncidenceFactor) applies on top.

rows.label: Ratio of average solar transmittance to that at normal incidence
rows.rationale: SAP 10.2 section 6, equation (5): solar gain = 0.9 × window area × solar flux × g⊥ × frame factor × solar access factor.

rows.label: Internal gains per m² of floor area
rows.rationale: Internal gains are a floor-area term plus a per-occupant term (gains.perOccupant). Both are fitted by least squares to SAP 10.2 Table 5 column (A) over 50–150 m², with N from Table 1b: metabolic 60N, cooking 35 + 7N, losses −40N, appliances from equation (L16), lighting from Appendix L at an assumed 50 lm/W, and 7 W of central heating pump. The fit is within 15 W of SAP across that range; it gives about 390 W for the 1930s semi with 3 occupants (phase 1 used 450 W).

rows.label: Internal gains per occupant
rows.rationale: The per-occupant term of the SAP 10.2 Table 5 fit (see gains.perFloorArea). The range, about ±30%, covers households with more or fewer appliances and more or less time at home. Correlated with hot water use per occupant through gains.perOccupantHotWaterCorrelation.

rows.label: Correlation of internal gains and hot water use per occupant
rows.rationale: No source gives this correlation. 0.5 assumes a household that is home more uses both more appliances and more hot water, without the two moving together exactly. It is in normal-score space (the Gaussian copula); the correlation of the drawn values is slightly lower. The sensitivity table moves each row alone, ignoring this correlation.

rows.label: Heating setpoint: air temperature during heating periods (calibrated to measured gas use)

source.title: DESNZ National Energy Efficiency Data-Framework (NEED) 2026 consumption data tables

rows.rationale: An air temperature, not an operative one, held during the heating periods of heating.scheduleGas; outside them the heating is off and the house cools against its thermal mass. Calibrated so the 1930s semi's central annual gas use (space heat plus hot water, divided by heating.boilerSeasonalEfficiency, with hot water from the hotWater rows and no cylinder loss for the combi) is 13,200 kWh, the midpoint of NEED's readings for comparable homes; the result must stay within their 10,980–15,433 kWh range. The target was fixed on 17 October 2026, before the engine existed, and the phase 2 spec fixed it again for the schedule before this calibration. 17.6 °C solves that target with the hourly engine, its thermal-mass node and SAP's schedule on the PVGIS typical year, with the archetype's derived geometry, its default answers (filled cavity walls, 100 mm of loft insulation) and every other row at its default (npm run calibrate; solved 17.56 °C on 20 October 2026, rounded to 0.1 °C). The low and high (16.2 and 18.8 °C) are the setpoints that reproduce NEED's readings A (10,980 kWh) and C (15,433 kWh) by the same method: they describe uncertainty about the typical home, not the spread between households. The schedule is not fitted; it stays at SAP's pattern. The spec's plausible range for the solved setpoint is 16–21 °C. It is below SAP's 21 °C living area because it stands for the whole house, and because the calibration may absorb fabric error from pessimistic RdSAP U-values as well as heating behaviour. It comes from gas-heated homes and applies to every archetype and to both setups, gas and heat pump ('the same household, different kit'). Phase 1 calibrated a continuous mean internal temperature instead (16.3 °C), which this row replaces; see the heating schedules ADR.
rows.overrideHint: Higher if you keep the house warmer when the heating is on; lower if you heat only some rooms.

rows.label: Heating periods for the gas setups, by hour of the week (1 heating, 0 off)
rows.rationale: SAP's heating pattern. Weekdays: 07:00–09:00 and 16:00–23:00, 9 hours (SAP 10.2 Table 9, note a). Weekends: 07:00–23:00, 16 hours, as the phase 2 spec sets: SAP's unimodal day (SAP 10.2 Table N7, note b). SAP 10.2's own Table 9 uses the two-period day on every day of the week, so this adds 14 heated hours a week to SAP 10.2's pattern. Monday 00:00 first; each value covers the hour starting then. Hours are clock time, so UK local time, converted to engine hours by the calendar module. Outside the periods the heating is off and the house cools against its thermal mass. Checked against the PDF on 20 October 2026.

rows.label: Heating periods for the heat pump setups, by hour of the week (1 heating, 0 off)
rows.rationale: 07:00–23:00 every day: SAP's unimodal day (SAP 10.2 Table N7, note b), which SAP's Appendix N gives heat pumps on their days of longer heating, in place of the gas setups' two periods on weekdays. No source gives heat pump heating hours by hour of the week, so this is SAP's longer heat pump day applied every day, chosen by Magnus on 20 October 2026 from three options (the gas schedule, this, and every hour). The evidence: on the gas schedule the capped heat pump can't recover after each off period, so the 1930s semi runs about 2 K colder on cold days and uses 6.7% less heat than the boiler house; the Electrification of Heat homes (about 545 air source heat pumps, daily data) cool only about 0.7 K from mild to cold days; and most HeatpumpMonitor.org systems run on weather compensation without room influence, which normally means no time schedule. A HEM check, with its rules committed before the run, puts the engine 2.4% below HEM on this schedule against 4.3% above on SAP's, so the engine understates the heat pump's space heat against the boiler's by about 6.7 points, in the heat pump's favour. That bias is stated wherever results are shown. Hours are clock time, so UK local time, converted to engine hours by the calendar module. Not tuned to favour either setup. On the gas schedule instead, the central 1930s semi's heat pump costs £1,911 a year rather than £1,967; the phase 2 report shows this comparison as the row's sensitivity.

rows.label: Gas combi boiler seasonal efficiency (space heat and hot water)
rows.rationale: Typical in-use seasonal efficiency of a condensing gas combi boiler serving a 1930s house. Condensing boilers rarely reach their rated 89–92% at radiator flow temperatures of 60–70 °C. Low 0.80 for a poorly set-up or older boiler; high 0.89 for a well-set-up boiler at lower flow temperatures. One efficiency covers both space heat and hot water. Gas is on a gross calorific value basis, as billed.
rows.overrideHint: Your boiler's seasonal efficiency, if known (for example from the Product Characteristics Database).

rows.label: Air source heat pump seasonal performance factor (space heat and hot water combined)

source.title: Energy Systems Catapult: Electrification of Heat interim heat pump performance data analysis report (2023)

rows.rationale: Fitted to field data. The Electrification of Heat trial's median air source SPF is 2.8; RHI monitoring found about 30% of air source heat pumps at 3.0 or above and about 8% at 3.5. A lognormal with median 2.8 and sigma 0.145 gives about 32% above 3.0 and 6% above 3.5, clipped to 2.0–4.0. The EoH figure is a whole-system SPF that includes hot water, so one SPF covers both uses and no separate hot water efficiency row is added; the boundary is H4, which includes the circulation pumps and any backup heater (interim analysis report, Table 11.1: median SPFH4 2.80, interquartile range 2.53–3.09, 291 air source heat pumps; the lognormal's own interquartile range is 2.54–3.09). HeatpumpMonitor's figure of about 4.0 is a self-selected sample, kept for phase 2's 'well-installed' option rather than this range.
rows.overrideHint: Your heat pump's measured SPF, for example from its monitoring app over a full year.

rows.label: Air source heat pump SPF, well-installed scenario (space heat and hot water combined)
rows.rationale: Air source heat pumps on HeatpumpMonitor.org with a full year of data and no data-quality flag (379 systems, fetched 19 October 2026): median combined COP 3.93, 10th to 90th percentile 3.23–4.54, standard deviation of the log 0.143. The combined COP includes hot water and, for nearly all systems, the central heating pumps, so it is on about the same H4 boundary as heating.heatPumpSpf. A lognormal with median 3.9 and sigma 0.14, clipped at about its 1st and 99th percentiles (2.8–5.4). The sample is self-selected: owners who monitor and publish their systems, often installed or tuned by enthusiasts. So this is a 'well-installed' scenario, not a forecast for a typical installation; the report labels it so.

source.title: HeatpumpMonitor.org public system statistics, last 365 days (fetched 19 October 2026)

rows.label: Heat pump COP curve: lift allowance added to the flow-to-outdoor difference
rows.rationale: The refrigerant condenses a few kelvin above the flow temperature and evaporates several kelvin below the outdoor air, so the compressor's lift is larger than flow minus outdoor. 10 K is a typical sum of the two approach temperatures. It shapes the curve only: k scales its level to the sampled SPF.

rows.label: Heat pump COP curve: lowest value of the unscaled shape
rows.rationale: Clamps the Carnot-like shape in the coldest hours at the highest flow temperatures. 4 sits just below the shape at −10 °C outdoors and a 55 °C flow, so it rarely binds, and at the lowest k the sampled SPFs give, it keeps the scaled COP above 1.

rows.label: Heat pump COP curve: highest value of the unscaled shape
rows.rationale: Clamps the Carnot-like shape when the outdoor temperature nears the flow temperature, where the ratio grows without limit. Real heat pumps gain little in mild weather because they cycle and run at minimum output. 15 is about the shape at a 25 °C flow and 15 °C outdoors.

rows.label: Heat pump COP: physical ceiling on the scaled COP
rows.rationale: No air source heat pump in normal operation sustains a COP much above 7, even at low flow temperatures in mild weather. If k would take any hour above 7, those hours run at 7 and k is re-solved so the year still matches the SPF.

rows.label: Heat pump standby electricity, as a share of its yearly electricity (field trial)

source.title: Electrification of Heat Demonstration Project: heat pump performance cleansed data, daily dataset 2020–2023 (UK Data Service SN 9210)

rows.rationale: Controls, circulation pumps and standby (including any crankcase heater): what an air source heat pump system draws on days it delivers almost no heat (under 0.5 kWh). For each of 308 air source heat pumps in the trial's daily data with at least 10 such days, its median idle-day electricity × 365 ÷ its yearly whole-system electricity. Across homes: median 5.9%, interquartile range 3.3–9.4%, 90th percentile 19% (the median idle day is 0.56 kWh). A lognormal with median 0.059 and sigma 0.78 (from the interquartile range), clipped to 0.01–0.25; the clip, not the sigma, limits the tail, and it keeps the share below 1 − SPF ÷ COP ceiling at the SPF's high. It sits inside the H4 boundary of heating.heatPumpSpf, so it does not add to the year's electricity: standby = this share × heat ÷ SPF, drawn evenly in every hour, and k is solved on the rest. A share, not kWh a day, so the solve works for every house size; small houses therefore get less standby in kWh than the trial's typical home, and their mild hours stay a little optimistic. The downloaded data is kept outside the repository under its end user licence; only these aggregates are recorded.

rows.label: Heat pump standby electricity, as a share of its yearly electricity (well-installed scenario)

source.title: HeatpumpMonitor.org public system statistics, last 365 days (fetched 19 October 2026)

rows.rationale: The same quantity for the well-installed scenario, so its standby matches its SPF's sample. For the 379 air source systems behind heating.heatPumpSpfWellInstalled: (combined electricity − electricity while running) ÷ combined electricity over the year. Median 2.5%, interquartile range 1.6–3.7%, 90th percentile 5.2%. A lognormal with median 0.025 and sigma 0.62, clipped to 0.005–0.10. Used only in the well-installed scenario, in place of heating.heatPumpStandbyShare. Self-selected, like the SPF it goes with.

rows.label: Weather compensation: outdoor temperature at which the flow reaches its design value
rows.rationale: About the outdoor design temperature UK heat loss calculations use for London (−2 to −3 °C). Colder hours keep the design flow temperature.

rows.label: Weather compensation: outdoor temperature at which the flow reaches its mild value
rows.rationale: About the outdoor temperature above which a house needs little heating. Milder hours keep the mild flow temperature.

rows.label: Heat pump space heating flow temperature at the design outdoor temperature
rows.rationale: Installers in the UK commonly design for 45 °C at the design temperature; 35 °C is an underfloor or oversized-radiator system and 50 °C a system that kept small radiators. Checked against field data: the Electrification of Heat trial's mean operating flow temperature was 38.3 °C over the year, including hot water, with 26 of 291 heat pumps averaging 45–55 °C (interim analysis report, section 8.3); on HeatpumpMonitor.org (19 October 2026), the median mean flow on each system's coldest day was 37 °C (10th to 90th percentile 32–43 °C). This line's heat-weighted mean flow is in engine.md. On the price cap it changes only when electricity is used, not how much, because k scales the year to the SPF.
rows.overrideHint: The flow temperature your heat pump runs at on the coldest days.

source.title: Energy Systems Catapult: Electrification of Heat interim heat pump performance data analysis report (2023)

rows.label: Heat pump space heating flow temperature at the mild outdoor temperature
rows.rationale: A weather-compensation curve typically falls to 25–35 °C in mild weather. On HeatpumpMonitor.org (19 October 2026), the median of each system's mean space heating flow over the year was 32 °C.
rows.overrideHint: The flow temperature your heat pump runs at in mild weather.

rows.label: Gas boiler pump and fan electricity
rows.rationale: SAP 10.2 Table 4f: a circulation pump from 2013 or later (41 kWh a year) plus a gas boiler's fan-assisted flue (45 kWh a year). v1 assumes the boiler is replaced now, and a new combi has an integral, modern pump. It is spread over the year in proportion to the boiler's gas use.
rows.overrideHint: Your boiler's pump and fan electricity, if known.

rows.label: Gas combi boiler: maximum space heating output
rows.rationale: Combi boilers for a typical house are rated about 24–35 kW for hot water, and most are range-rated to about 18–24 kW for space heating. 24 kW is well above the design heat loss of every archetype (at most about 10 kW, for the pre-1900 end-terrace at its defaults), so the cap rarely binds; it limits only the recovery after the heating has been off. The engine caps the boiler's space heat output at this; hot water is outside the cap. A very large or poorly insulated house beyond the archetypes could exceed it, and would then need a larger boiler row.

rows.label: Design temperature difference for the design heat loss
rows.rationale: SAP 10.2 Appendix N, section N2: the dwelling's design heat loss is its heat loss coefficient × 24.2 K, used for a heat pump's plant size ratio. About 21 °C inside and −3 °C outside. London's design temperature is a little milder (about −2 °C), so this gives a slightly larger heat pump. Checked against the PDF on 20 October 2026.

rows.label: Heat pump rated output ÷ design heat loss
rows.rationale: The median ratio of rated heat pump output to the installer's design heat loss for 747 air source systems on HeatpumpMonitor.org with both figures (fetched 20 October 2026): median 1.15, 10th to 90th percentile 0.89–1.60. HeatpumpMonitor.org is a self-selected sample of engaged owners, so this may be a little generous. The engine caps the heat pump's space heating output at this × the design heat loss: a simple limit, not a sizing method, and there is no backup heater.

rows.label: Hot water delivery temperature
rows.rationale: A typical tap and shower delivery temperature from a combi boiler or a heat pump cylinder.

rows.label: Cold water feed temperature (annual average)
rows.rationale: Annual average mains temperature in southern England. Monthly variation is phase 2.

rows.label: Hot water cylinder standing loss (heat pump setup only)
rows.rationale: A typical declared standing loss for a 200-litre factory-insulated heat pump cylinder; manufacturers' figures are about 1.2–1.9 kWh a day. The gas setup is a combi boiler and has no cylinder.
rows.overrideHint: The declared heat loss on your cylinder's label.

rows.label: Hot water use, fixed part per household
rows.rationale: SAP 2012's hot water formula, 25 × occupants + 36 litres a day, which phase 1 used at the delivery temperature. SAP 10.2 replaced it with a shower-and-bath calculation (Appendix J) that needs data the quick facts do not ask.

rows.label: Hot water use per occupant
rows.rationale: The per-occupant term of SAP 2012's 25 × occupants + 36 (see hotWater.litresBase). The range, about ±30%, covers lighter and heavier users. For the 1930s semi's 3 occupants it gives 111 litres a day, 78–141 across the range (phase 1 used 100, 70–140).

rows.label: Heat pump flow temperature when heating the hot water cylinder
rows.rationale: The mean flow temperature while the heat pump heats the cylinder. On HeatpumpMonitor.org (19 October 2026), the median system's mean hot water flow was 45 °C, for a median cylinder target of 48 °C: the flow starts low and ends a few kelvin above the cylinder. With this register's 50 °C setpoint that suggests about 47 °C; 50 °C is a little pessimistic, and keeps the hot water flow at or above every space heating flow (the design flow's high is 50 °C), so hot water is never the cheaper duty.

source.title: HeatpumpMonitor.org public system statistics, last 365 days (fetched 19 October 2026)

rows.label: Hot water cylinder volume (heat pump setups only)
rows.rationale: A common size for a heat pump cylinder in a three-bedroom house, and the size hotWater.cylinderStandingLoss describes.

rows.label: Hot water cylinder setpoint (heat pump setups only)
rows.rationale: A common heat pump cylinder setting, which keeps the flow temperature and so the COP penalty low. Legionella cycles are not modelled.

rows.label: Hot water cylinder reheat trigger (heat pump setups only)
rows.rationale: The cylinder is reheated to its setpoint when it falls below this, a 5 K hysteresis that is a common controller default. The engine holds the cylinder as one stored-energy state, not a stratified tank, so this is a reheat trigger, not a tap temperature: the draw-off takes the heat the taps need (hotWater.deliveryTemperature) whatever the state.

rows.label: Hot water draw-off by hour of the day (share of the day's hot water)
rows.rationale: The whole-sample hourly energy profile of about 120 English homes (Figure 6.9). The hours 07:00–22:00 use the report's own tapping cycle (Table A3.2, kWh); the hours 23:00–06:00, which that table folds into one early-morning draw, are read from Figure 6.9 (MJ). The night hours read from the figure sum to 0.531 kWh, against the table's 0.529, so the two agree. Shares of the 4.65 kWh day, rounded to 4 decimals so they sum to 1. Hours are clock time, so UK local time, converted to engine hours by the calendar module. Combi and regular boiler homes had very similar profiles (Figure 6.6), so one profile serves both setups.

source.title: Measurement of domestic hot water consumption in dwellings (Energy Saving Trust for Defra, 2008)

rows.label: Electricity unit rate, price cap, GB average, Direct Debit, 1 October–31 December 2026

source.title: Ofgem: Energy price cap unit rates and standing charges

rows.rationale: Electricity carries no VAT from October 2026 to March 2027.
rows.overrideHint: The unit rate on your electricity bill.

rows.label: Electricity standing charge, price cap, GB average, Direct Debit, 1 October–31 December 2026

source.title: Ofgem: Energy price cap unit rates and standing charges

rows.rationale: Paid by both setups.
rows.overrideHint: The standing charge on your electricity bill.

rows.label: Gas unit rate, price cap, GB average, Direct Debit, 1 October–31 December 2026

source.title: Ofgem: Energy price cap unit rates and standing charges

rows.rationale: Includes 5% VAT. Per kWh on a gross calorific value basis, as billed.
rows.overrideHint: The unit rate on your gas bill.

rows.label: Gas standing charge, price cap, GB average, Direct Debit, 1 October–31 December 2026

source.title: Ofgem: Energy price cap unit rates and standing charges

rows.rationale: Includes 5% VAT. Paid only by the gas setup: the heat-pump-only house is assumed to have no gas hob and no gas supply.
rows.overrideHint: The standing charge on your gas bill.

rows.label: Export rate for solar setups, flat, London

source.title: Octopus Energy public API: Outgoing Octopus (OUTGOING-VAR-24-10-26), London region (C) unit rates

rows.rationale: Approximate until the tariffs PR snapshots the Octopus rates; the source is the API query the mode was taken from on 19 October 2026. The range spans the export tariffs a solar household in London can get from Octopus, as Magnus decided on 20 October 2026: the low end is Octopus's fixed Smart Export Guarantee tariff (4.1p/kWh since February 2022), the mode is Outgoing Octopus, the flat tariff the spec calls Outgoing Fixed (12p/kWh in London from 1 March 2026), and the high end is Outgoing Octopus's earlier rate (15p/kWh from October 2024 to February 2026). All are flat, with no VAT and no standing charge. Triangular, so the mean is 10.4p. The engine assumes every solar setup qualifies for the tariff it is drawn.
rows.overrideHint: The export rate on your export tariff.

rows.label: Real change in gas prices each year, after inflation
rows.rationale: No forecast is reliable over a heat pump's lifetime. The default of no real change keeps today's prices; −3% to +3% a year spans a long fall back towards pre-2021 prices and a sustained rise such as a carbon price on gas. Drawn once per sample and applied to every year after the first, to both the unit rate and the standing charge. Symmetric, so the range favours neither fuel.

rows.label: Real change in electricity prices each year, after inflation
rows.rationale: As prices.gasRealChange: no real change by default, −3% to +3% a year, symmetric. A fall would follow cheaper renewables or moving policy costs off electricity bills; a rise would follow network investment costs. Applied to the unit rate, the standing charge and the export rate.

rows.label: Correlation of the gas and electricity real price changes
rows.rationale: No source gives this correlation. Gas-fired power often sets the wholesale electricity price in Great Britain, so the two tend to move together, but not exactly: policy costs, network costs and a growing share of renewables move electricity on its own. 0.6 is in normal-score space (the Gaussian copula). The sensitivity table moves each row alone, ignoring this correlation.

rows.label: Natural gas carbon factor, gross calorific value (DESNZ 2026 factor set)

source.title: DESNZ: Greenhouse gas reporting: conversion factors 2026

rows.rationale: Scope 1 combustion factor for natural gas per kWh on a gross CV basis, which matches billed gas. The value is the recent editions' figure: DESNZ's 2026 summaries say fuel factors are mostly unchanged, but the exact 2026 cell in the full-set spreadsheet still needs checking. Well-to-tank emissions are excluded, as for electricity.

rows.label: Grid electricity carbon factor, annual average, electricity consumed (DESNZ 2026 factor set, 2025 data year)

source.title: DESNZ: 2026 GHG conversion factors methodology paper, Table 9 (including imported electricity)

rows.rationale: Electricity consumed, which includes transmission and distribution losses: 0.13096 for generation plus 0.01299 for losses, given as 0.14396 in Table 9. Well-to-tank emissions are excluded. An annual average; the hourly grid profile is phase 2.

rows.label: Base electricity use (lights and appliances), the same in both setups

source.title: Ofgem: Review of typical domestic consumption values, decision (May 2026), Table 1

rows.rationale: Ofgem's 2026 typical consumption values for single-rate electricity meters: low 1,600, medium 2,500 and high 3,800 kWh a year, used as the low, mode and high. Unlike most ranges here, this one is the spread between households, not uncertainty about a typical home: it is kept because base use is the same in both setups and cancels out of the paired difference, but it widens each setup's own cost band. Checked against Table 1 of the decision on 17 October 2026. A gas-heated home on a single-rate meter is the typical case these values describe. The boiler's own pump and fan electricity is left out in phase 1.
rows.overrideHint: Your annual electricity use from your bills, less any electric heating or car charging.

rows.label: Base electricity use by hour of the week (shape, mean 1)

source.title: Elexon: average profiling data per profile class, 2013/14, evaluated at 10-year average temperatures

rows.rationale: Profile class 1 (domestic unrestricted) from Elexon's average profiling data for 2013/14, evaluated at 10-year average temperatures: half-hourly mean demand for five seasons × three day types (weekday, Saturday, Sunday). Each day type's hourly use is averaged over its days in the reference year 2026, using Elexon's season rules, so the shape is the year's average for that day type; bank holidays count as their weekday. The two half-hours of each hour are averaged. Hours are clock time, so UK local time, converted to engine hours by the calendar module. Scaled to a mean of 1 and rounded to 4 decimals; the engine multiplies it by the month level and rescales the year to the base use row. The shape changes little between seasons (the share of a weekday's use between 10:00 and 16:00 is 25.5% in winter and 26.4% in summer), which is why one weekly shape and a month level stand in for the fifteen season and day-type profiles. Derived by `npm run derive:base-profile` from the downloaded file, which is not committed.

rows.label: Base electricity use by month (level, mean 1 over the year's days)

source.title: Elexon: average profiling data per profile class, 2013/14, evaluated at 10-year average temperatures

rows.rationale: Each month's mean daily use in profile class 1, from the same data and season rules as the weekly shape, divided by the year's mean daily use and rounded to 4 decimals. Winter days use about a third more than summer days (lighting and some electric heating in the class). Months are UK local time.

rows.label: Roof solar PV system size before the roof limit
rows.rationale: The spec's default of 4 kWp, a common size for a domestic roof in England; 2.5 to 6 kWp spans the systems typically fitted to houses. The sampled size is clipped to the roof's maximum (see solar.usableRoofFraction), so on a small roof the upper part of the range gives the roof's maximum, and the usable roof fraction's range then sets the spread of sizes.
rows.overrideHint: The size of the system you have or have been quoted, in kWp.

rows.label: Roof solar PV tilt, which is also the roof pitch
rows.rationale: A typical pitched roof in England is 30–45°; 35° is the spec's default. Panels lie flat on the roof, so the tilt is also the pitch used for the roof's maximum system size.
rows.overrideHint: Your roof's pitch.

rows.label: Roof solar PV direction
rows.rationale: Panels go on the roof slope that faces closest to south. A house's best slope faces anywhere from south-east to south-west, so the range is −45° (south-east) to +45° (south-west) with south as the mode. This lets the sensitivity table show how much roof direction matters. Uses Duffie and Beckman's convention, as PVGIS's aspect does.
rows.overrideHint: The direction your best roof slope faces.

rows.label: Roof solar PV system loss (inverter, cables, mismatch and soiling)

source.title: PVGIS user manual: PV system loss

rows.rationale: PVGIS's suggested default system loss of 14%, which covers losses between the modules and the house but not reflection, spectral or temperature effects. The engine models temperature separately and leaves out reflection and spectral effects, which the PVGIS check measures.

rows.label: PV module power temperature coefficient
rows.rationale: Crystalline silicon modules lose about 0.3–0.45% of their output per K of cell temperature above 25 °C, by their datasheets; −0.4% per K is a middle value for the modules on English roofs.

rows.label: PV cell temperature above air temperature, per W/m² on the panel
rows.rationale: The nominal operating cell temperature (NOCT) model: a module with a NOCT of 45 °C runs (45 − 20) ÷ 800 = 0.031 K above the air per W/m² (the standard NOCT relation, leaving out the small efficiency term and wind). NOCT describes an open-rack module, so the PVGIS check uses PVGIS's free-standing mounting.

rows.label: Share of one roof slope that panels can cover
rows.rationale: Panels keep clear of the roof's edges, ridge and hips, and of vents and roof windows. 70% of one slope is an estimate for a simple pitched roof; 50% allows for a hipped roof, a dormer or roof windows, and 85% for a plain gable roof laid out edge to edge. It is uncertain because it decides the roof's maximum, which clips the system size on most of the house types.

rows.label: PV peak power per m² of covered roof
rows.rationale: A current 400–430 W module measures about 1.7 × 1.13 m (1.95 m²), so about 0.21 kWp per m² of module; 0.2 allows for the gaps between modules.

rows.label: Replacement gas combi boiler, installed
rows.rationale: No official statistics cover boiler installation costs, so this is an assumption to replace with a sourced figure. £3,000 is taken as a typical like-for-like combi swap with a system flush and a magnetic filter; £2,000 a basic swap in an easy position, and £4,500 a larger boiler or one that moves. It counts against every gas setup, and again each time the boiler's lifetime ends inside the payback horizon.
rows.overrideHint: The quote you have for a replacement boiler.

rows.label: Air source heat pump, installed, with its cylinder and typical radiator changes, before the grant

source.title: DESNZ: Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics, August 2026 (table Q1.1A)

rows.rationale: Reported costs of air-to-water heat pumps redeemed under the Boiler Upgrade Scheme in England and Wales, 2026 Q2: median £12,908, interquartile range £11,128–£15,627. The statistics' note 4: costs come from the MCS certificate, are self-reported by installers, include the system, labour and VAT, and should include the grant value (so they are before the grant, though installers may interpret this differently); the highest and lowest 10% are excluded. So the true spread is wider than these quartiles, and the clip limits allow for that. The statistics don't say whether the cost covers the hot water cylinder and radiator changes; the engine assumes the reported cost is the whole installation, including them. A lognormal with median £12,900 and sigma 0.25 gives an interquartile range of £10,900–£15,300; clipped to £8,000–£22,000. One row for every archetype: the 2025/26 medians by capacity range from £11,494 (4–6 kW) to £13,943 (10–12 kW), inside this range.
rows.overrideHint: The quote you have for a heat pump, before the grant.

rows.label: Roof solar PV system, installed, per kWp

source.title: DESNZ: Solar PV cost data, 2025/26 (Total Installed Capacity file, summary and domestic tables)

rows.rationale: MCS-registered installations in 2025/26: median £1,595 per kW for 0–4 kW systems and £1,546 for 4–10 kW. These medians include non-domestic installations, which cost less: the 0–4 kW mean is £1,955 for domestic installations and £1,650 for non-domestic ones, against £1,808 for all. No domestic median is published, so the mode scales the 0–4 kW median by the domestic-to-all ratio of means (1,955 ÷ 1,808): about £1,700. A triangular with mode £1,700 and range £1,250–£2,500. The cost includes the panels, inverter, installation, connection and VAT where it applies, and excludes batteries. Applied to the system size after the roof limit, so the fixed part of a small system's cost is not captured.
rows.overrideHint: Your solar quote divided by its size in kWp.

rows.label: Boiler Upgrade Scheme grant for an air source heat pump, England and Wales

source.title: GOV.UK: Apply for the Boiler Upgrade Scheme (what you can get, and check if you're eligible)

rows.rationale: £7,500 towards an air source heat pump, checked on GOV.UK on 19 October 2026. The extra £1,500 until March 2027 is only for oil or LPG homes with no mains gas, so it does not apply: every v1 home has mains gas. The conditions, as GOV.UK lists them: the applicant owns the property (including second homes and rented-out homes); the heat pump replaces a fossil fuel system such as gas; it is installed and commissioned within 120 days of the application; the property has not had government funding for a heat pump or biomass boiler before; social housing and most new builds are excluded; and the system is at most 45 kWth. GOV.UK sets no EPC or insulation condition. The Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics (August 2026, 'Scheme background') add that the installer applies and is paid the grant, must deduct it from the owner's price, and that every installation must be MCS-certified; the engine assumes that certification, and the same for PV export payments. The engine applies the grant to heat pump setups only, capped at the installed cost, and never to a replacement heat pump (a property that has had the grant cannot claim it again).

rows.label: Air source heat pump lifetime
rows.rationale: No field data yet covers a full lifetime of today's air source heat pumps; 15–20 years is the span commonly quoted. A triangular with mode 18 and range 13–22 years. Rounded to whole years, it is the payback horizon for heat pump setups. Its upper end is no later than solar PV's lower end, and a lifetime ending at the horizon is not replaced, so PV never needs replacing inside a heat pump horizon.

rows.label: Gas combi boiler lifetime
rows.rationale: 10–15 years is the span commonly quoted for a combi boiler. A triangular with mode 13 and range 10–16 years. Rounded to whole years. The reference boiler is replaced again whenever its lifetime ends inside the payback horizon, at today's real cost.

rows.label: Roof solar PV system lifetime
rows.rationale: Panel output warranties commonly run 25 years, and panels often last longer. A triangular with mode 25 and range 22–30 years. Rounded to whole years, it is the payback horizon for gas with solar and for solar's own payback. An inverter replacement partway through is not modelled, which flatters solar slightly.
